analysis.one_liner: Penalizes opioid makers and executives for misleading marketing, and funds addiction treatment with the money collected.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2021, having attracted just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for opioid makers and distributors to falsely advertise opioids as non-addictive, to ship communities quantities they know are not medically reasonable, or to ignore suspicious order patterns. Companies that violated it could owe 75 percent of their opioid profits, executives could personally owe their salaries plus stock gains and face prison time, and the industry would owe a total of $20 billion in fees. The money would fund addiction treatment, prevention, and services for affected families, and companies caught violating the rules would lose exclusive rights to sell their opioid drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic: the $20 billion fund would pay for treatment, prevention, school programs, Head Start trauma care, and services for affected families. Patients would also gain if losing market exclusivity opened opioids and other drugs to cheaper generic competition. People with pain would benefit from tighter controls on oversupply that contributed to addiction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families and communities hit by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal violation to falsely market opioids as non-addictive, to supply communities with quantities a person knows are not medically reasonable, or to fail to report suspicious distribution orders.

Imposes real personal consequences: employees of opioid makers and distributors face civil penalties equal to their salary plus stock gains during the violation period and up to 10 years in prison, and CEOs and other executives are personally penalized even if they claim not to have known about the violation.

Assesses a total of $20 billion in fees on every company that manufactured or distributed opioids covered by federal health programs between 1993 and enactment, with companies that don't pay losing FDA approval for their drugs.

Puts the penalties and fees into a fund for opioid misuse treatment and prevention, with priority for programs serving people directly affected and their families, school prevention programs, and Head Start trauma-informed child care.
Strips market exclusivity from companies found in violation, halving exclusivity on their other drugs and blocking 'product hopping' reformulations, which would let cheaper generic competitors in.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers and distributors, which could owe civil penalties of 75 percent of their U.S. opioid profits during violation periods plus a share of a $20 billion fee; and their executives, who would personally owe their salaries plus stock gains from those periods and face imprisonment. Some cost could pass to patients and taxpayers if penalties disrupted supply or drove companies toward bankruptcy before victims were compensated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid manufacturers, distributors, and their executives

drawbacks.text: The $20 billion fee applies retroactively to conduct dating back to 1993, and the executive penalties apply 'without regard to' an individual's participation in or knowledge of the violation — a due-process problem that a court challenge could tie up for years, delaying money for treatment.

Companies that fail to pay the fee lose FDA approval for their drugs, and a 75-percent-of-profits penalty could push an opioid maker into bankruptcy; in past opioid cases, bankruptcy complicated and slowed compensation for victims and could disrupt the supply of legitimate pain medication for patients who need it.

The bill leaves key terms to later agency decisions — HHS must write the formula for what quantity is 'not medically reasonable' and set each company's fee through rulemaking — so the actual burden on any one company was undefined at introduction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — money and accountability for the communities devastated by the opioid epidemic, paid by the companies and executives who profited — is genuine, and the design goes further than most accountability bills by clawing back executive pay and stock gains. But the harshest provisions were drafted in a way that invites constitutional challenge and could push companies into bankruptcy courts where victims have historically waited years for payment, and the blanket treatment of executives regardless of knowledge is the weakest part. A narrower, more litigation-proof version might have delivered less money faster.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee, and it sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, joined by Rep. Ro Khanna as its only cosponsor.
The Speaker referred it to two committees — Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor — a dual referral that requires two committees to act before a bill can move.

One day later it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and the record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with 2 total sponsors out of 435 House members.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers and distributors and their executives came out ahead: they never faced the 75-percent-of-profits penalties, the $20 billion fee, the executive pay clawbacks, or the loss of market exclusivity. Communities affected by the epidemic gained nothing, because the treatment fund was never created.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows its referral to the Health Subcommittee on May 23, 2019 and no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill never built caucus support: its two sponsors were both Democrats, but only 1 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored and no Democratic-controlled committee acted on it.

industries.industry: Opioid manufacturers (e.g. makers of prescription painkillers)
industries.note: The bill hits them hardest: civil penalties of 75 percent of U.S. opioid profits during violation periods, a share of a $20 billion industry-wide fee, revocation of market exclusivity on opioid drugs, and halved exclusivity on their other drugs. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the communities the fund would have served.

Distributors that shipped medically unreasonable quantities or failed to report suspicious orders would face the same corporate penalties and would pay part of the $20 billion fee, since the fee covers any entity that manufactured or distributed federally covered opioids since 1993.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical executives (CEOs and finance, research, marketing, and sales chiefs)
industries.note: The bill pierces the corporate shield: CEOs would personally owe their salary plus stock gains from violation periods, other senior executives 25 percent of each, regardless of whether they sold the stock or knew of the violation, with prison terms for employees involved.
Revoking and halving market exclusivity for violators and banning 'product hopping' reformulations would open markets to cheaper generic competition sooner.
